newsitem.title: USA: Fla. may shift $2.2 billion from prisons to school.
newsitem.headline: Fla. may shift $2.2 billion from prisons to school.

text.p: Florida will need 32,000 fewer prison beds than originally projected in five years, which could allow it to shift $2.2 billion from prison construction to other programs, according to a legislative report.

Earlier forecasts projected Florida would need to house 116,205 prisoners by 2002. In revised estimates reported to legislative leaders Monday, the Joint Legislative Management Committee cut the figure to 84,009.

As a result, lawmakers are considering a plan to slow prison building and instead use up to $2.2 billion for school construction and social programs. Senate analysts said savings in fiscal 1998 alone could be as much as $202 million.
The original estimates were based on sentencing patterns before 1995, when Florida enacted a law requiring prisoners to serve at least 85 percent of their sentences.
Until then, Florida prisons were so crowded that the state was required to release most prisoners after they had served only one-third of their sentences.
The change sparked a prison building boom. But the percentage of convicted defendats sentenced to prison dropped from 19 percent in 1994 to 14 percent in 1996.
Analysts quoted Tuesday in the Fort Lauderdale Sun-Sentinel said that may be because prosecutors are using the tougher guidelines to get plea bargains from defendants.

They said judges may also be adjusting sentencing strategies. Before the law changed, they may have been more likely to exceed sentencing guidelines because they knew prisoners would serve only a small portion of the sentence. Now that they are confident prisoners will serve most of their terms, judges may be handing down shorter terms, the analysts said.
